traps.snippet:
IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#txn') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #txn;

        SELECT  t.txn_id, t.policy_id, UPPER(RTRIM(t.txn_type)) AS txn_type, t.txn_date,
                t.effective_from, t.effective_to, t.currency, t.amount,
                CAST(1 AS DECIMAL(18,8)) AS fx_rate
        INTO    #txn
traps.note: The #txn temp table is built with SELECT INTO and then added to by an INSERT; in Spark it becomes a DataFrame made by unioning the EUR and non-EUR branches.
currency is CHAR(3) text. Under a CI collation, 'eur' or 'Eur' also matches 'EUR', but Spark's binary compare would drop those rows from the EUR branch.
currency is CHAR(3), and SQL Server ignores trailing spaces in the comparison. A value like 'EU ' or a padded source value would compare differently in Spark.

traps.snippet:
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 r.rate_to_eur
                     FROM   stg.fx_rates r WITH (NOLOCK)
                     WHERE  r.currency = t.currency
                       AND  r.rate_date <= t.txn_date
                     ORDER BY r.rate_date DESC, r._row_seq DESC) fx
traps.note: TOP 1 is ordered by rate_date DESC, _row_seq DESC. If _row_seq ties within a date, the row chosen is arbitrary, so the window ordering must match.

traps.snippet:
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 r.rate_to_eur
                     FROM   stg.fx_rates r WITH (NOLOCK)
                     WHERE  r.currency = t.currency
                       AND  r.rate_date <= t.txn_date
                     ORDER BY r.rate_date DESC, r._row_seq DESC) fx
traps.note: CROSS APPLY TOP 1 picks the latest rate per transaction and drops transactions that have no rate. In Spark this needs a join with a row_number window (inner semantics).
The rate lookup joins on the CHAR(3) currency columns. The CI collation matches case variants such as 'usd' to 'USD', and Spark's join would miss them.
The CHAR(3) join on currency ignores trailing spaces in the legacy engine. Spark needs trimmed keys to match the same way.
The <> 'EUR' test is case-insensitive in the legacy engine. In Spark, lower-case 'eur' rows would go to the FX branch and also be missing from the EUR branch.
currency is CHAR(3) and the legacy comparison ignores trailing spaces. Spark compares the exact string.

traps.snippet: CAST(ROUND(x.amount * x.fx_rate, 2) AS DECIMAL(14,2)) AS written_eur,
traps.note: DECIMAL(12,2)*DECIMAL(18,8) is rounded half away from zero to 2 places and cast to DECIMAL(14,2). Spark must keep decimal types and HALF_UP rounding, not doubles.
earned_days*100/term_days is INT/INT, so the percentage is truncated to a whole number before it is stored in DECIMAL(5,2) (e.g. 33.00, not 33.33). Spark's / would return a fraction.
Decimal * int / 365 follows SQL Server's precision and scale rules for division, then ROUND to 2 places half away from zero. Spark's decimal division and rounding must reproduce this.
Unearned is written_eur minus the separately rounded earned amount, so the decimal scale and rounding of the subtrahend must match the legacy result.
ROUND(x, 4, 1) truncates rather than rounds. Spark needs an explicit truncation of the decimal quotient (e.g. floor-based for positive values, toward zero for negatives), not F.round.
term_days/30 is integer division, so the instalment count is truncated: 365 days gives 12, and under 30 days gives 0, which falls back to 1.
Decimal divided by an int count, then ROUND to 2 places half away from zero into DECIMAL(14,2). The decimal types must be kept.
DATEADD(MONTH,1,EOMONTH(d)) clamps without snapping to month-end: an end of February gives the 28th/29th of March. Spark's add_months on a last-day input returns the 31st, so the result would differ.
is_current is CHAR(1) text. Under the CI collation a lower-case 'y' also matches, and Spark's exact compare would drop those policies from the inner join.
is_current is CHAR(1). The trailing-space-insensitive compare is a latent risk only if values are stored with spaces.

contracts.grain: One row per premium transaction booked on or before the reporting date whose policy has a current row in dim_policy. Each row holds the written and earned premium in EUR as at @AsOfDate.

columns.name: fx_rate
columns.description: 1 for EUR. For other currencies it is the latest stg.fx_rates rate on or before txn_date; if two rows share a date, the higher _row_seq wins. Transactions with no rate found are dropped (CROSS APPLY).

columns.name: written_eur
columns.description: amount * fx_rate, rounded to 2 decimal places.

columns.name: term_days
columns.description: Days of cover counting both ends: DATEDIFF(effective_from, effective_to) + 1.

columns.name: earned_days
columns.description: Days of cover earned by as_of_date, between 0 and term_days.

columns.name: earned_pct
columns.description: Integer division earned_days*100/term_days, so it is truncated to a whole percent.

columns.name: earned_eur
columns.description: written_eur * earned_days / 365 (not / term_days), rounded to 2 dp. It can differ from written_eur even when fully earned.

columns.name: daily_rate_eur
columns.description: written_eur / term_days, truncated (not rounded) to 4 dp.

columns.name: monthly_instalment_eur
columns.description: written_eur divided by integer term_days/30, or by 1 if that is 0; rounded to 2 dp.

columns.name: first_due_date
columns.description: First day of the second month after effective_from (DATEADD month 1 to EOMONTH).

columns.name: as_of_date
columns.description: The @AsOfDate parameter; the same on every row.

defects.title: Earned premium pro-rated over a fixed 365 days instead of the policy term
defects.description: earned_eur = ROUND(written_eur * earned_days / 365, 2) and unearned_eur = written_eur - that. The denominator is hard-coded at 365 while term_days is computed right above. Leap-year terms (366 days), short-term policies and terms over a year are earned wrongly; a fully earned 366-day policy shows earned > written and negative unearned.
defects.intended_behaviour: earned_eur = ROUND(written_eur * earned_days / term_days, 2), so a fully earned policy earns exactly written_eur; unearned_eur = written_eur - earned_eur.

defects.title: Earned percentage truncated by integer division
defects.description: earned_pct = e.earned_days * 100 / e.term_days, where every operand is INT, so SQL Server does integer division and drops the fraction (e.g. 182*100/365 = 49 instead of 49.86) before storing into DECIMAL(5,2).
defects.intended_behaviour: earned_pct = ROUND(earned_days * 100.0 / term_days, 2), keeping two decimals.
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected, COALESCE(SUM(ABS(CAST(g.earned_pct AS DECIMAL(10,4)) - ROUND(CAST(g.earned_days AS DECIMAL(20,6)) * 100 / g.term_days, 2))), 0) AS amount_affected FROM golden_dw_fact_premium_earned g WHERE g.term_days <> 0 AND g.earned_pct <> ROUND(CAST(g.earned_days AS DECIMAL(20,6)) * 100 / g.term_days, 2)

defects.title: First instalment due date: month added to month-end gives an inconsistent date
defects.description: first_due_date = DATEADD(MONTH, 1, EOMONTH(effective_from)). This takes the last day of the effective month and adds a month, giving the end of next month sometimes (31 Jan -> 29 Feb) and not other times (28 Feb -> 28 Mar, 30 Apr -> 30 May). It is neither the 1st of the next month nor reliably the end of next month.
defects.intended_behaviour: Most likely the first day of the month after the effective month: DATEADD(DAY, 1, EOMONTH(effective_from)), or else EOMONTH(effective_from, 1).
defects.impact_query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_dw_fact_premium_earned g WHERE g.first_due_date <> DATE_ADD(LAST_DAY(g.effective_from), 1)

impact.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_affected FROM golden_dw_fact_premium_earned g WHERE g.first_due_date <> DATE_ADD(LAST_DAY(g.effective_from), 1)

defects.title: Non-EUR transactions without an FX rate on/before booking date silently dropped
defects.description: The non-EUR branch uses CROSS APPLY to the latest rate with rate_date <= txn_date. A transaction whose currency has no rate on or before its booking date (or has a NULL currency, which fails both = 'EUR' and <> 'EUR') produces no row at all, so the written premium disappears from the fact table without any error or log.
defects.intended_behaviour: Every transaction should be in the fact (full premium population). A missing rate should fall back (e.g. the earliest available rate) or fail/log the job rather than drop the premium.

defects.title: Transactions dropped when the policy has no current dim_policy row
defects.description: The final INSERT inner-joins to dw.dim_policy on is_current = 'Y'. Transactions for policies with no current version (not yet loaded, or the version-closing logic left none current) are silently excluded from the premium fact.
defects.intended_behaviour: All premium transactions up to the as-of date should be reported; a missing policy should map to an unknown member or be logged, not dropped.

tests.description: Currency case variants: 'eur' and 'Eur' rows belong to the EUR branch (lines 69/82). Under the CI collation they get rate 1, and they must not go to the FX branch. A naive binary compare would drop them, or send them looking for a rate. The FX join on line 79 must match txn 'usd' to fx 'USD', and txn 'GBP' to fx 'Gbp'. In dim_policy, policy 104 has is_current 'y' (line 134), so its rows join only under the CI compare. Canonical 'EUR'/'USD'/'Y' rows are included as controls, along with a non-current 'N' row.

Trailing spaces in CHAR(3) currency keys (lines 69/79/82). Txn currency 'CH' matches fx 'CH ', and txn 'JP ' matches fx 'JP'. The legacy engine pads both and ignores trailing spaces, so the rows find their rates. A naive exact-string join drops them. txn_type values carry trailing spaces ('NB  ', 'MTA '), and RTRIM removes them. Canonical 'EUR' and 'USD' rows are included as controls, and is_current is 'Y'.

FX TOP 1 tie-break (lines 77-81). USD has two rates on 2025-06-01 (0.92 at seq 2, a revision 0.93 at seq 4). GBP has two rates on 2025-06-01 (1.18 at seq 5, 1.17 at seq 6). The legacy engine picks the later _row_seq. A window ordered only by rate_date, or by insertion order, could pick the other row. A USD rate dated after some txn dates (2025-07-01, inserted first) must be ignored for those txns and used for a later txn. A txn on 2025-05-15 must take the older 0.91 rate. A EUR row is included as a control.

Decimal rounding, lines 92 and 125-128. Several amount*rate products land exactly on half a cent: 10.01*0.5=5.005, 2.35*1.5=3.525, -10.01*0.5=-5.005. Rounding half away from zero is required. Doubles or HALF_EVEN would differ. CHF 999.99*1.07123457 tests the full-precision product. Partial-term EUR rows (1000.00 over 184 of 365 days, 333.33 over a short term) test the /365 decimal scale and unearned = written - ROUND(...). A negative EUR -100.00 over 365 days tests ROUND(x,4,1) truncation toward zero for the daily rate (floor would differ). Other rows give non-terminating quotients for the daily rate and the instalment.

Integer division, lines 124 and 128. A 3-day term with 1 earned day gives an earned_pct of 1*100/3, truncated to 33 (not 33.33). A 90-day term with 31 days earned gives 34, not 34.44. A 151-day term with 31 days earned gives 20 (3100/151=20.53, so rounding would give 21). A future-dated term earns 0. A fully earned 365-day term is included as a control. Instalments: a 365-day term gives a count of 12 (not 12.17). A 20-day term gives 0, which falls back to 1. A 59-day term gives 1 and a 366-day term gives 12. All rows are EUR.

first_due_date = DATEADD(MONTH,1,EOMONTH(effective_from)), line 129. These effective_from dates have month-ends shorter than the following month: Feb 2025 (to Mar 28), Feb 2024 leap (to Mar 29), Apr 30 (to May 30), Jun 30 (to Jul 30), Sep (to Oct 30), Nov 30 (to Dec 30). The legacy engine does not snap to month-end, but a last-day-preserving add_months would return the 31st. Controls: January (clamps to Feb 28), Mar 31 (to Apr 30) and Dec 2025 (to Jan 31, 2026). All rows are EUR.

1) earned_pct = earned_days*100/term_days uses integer division in T-SQL. The value is cut down to a whole number, then stored as DECIMAL(5,2), so values like 33.00 appear, not 33.33.

For terms longer than 365 days, or when the cover period is fully earned, earned_eur can be more than written_eur, which makes unearned_eur negative. translator notes: I haven't run this module. Points to check in review:

1) first_due_date: the target month comes from add_months(last_day(d), 1). The day is then set to the smaller of the month-end day and the target month's last day. The result is right whichever way Spark's add_months handles month-end inputs.

2) Decimal divisions (earned_eur, daily_rate_eur, monthly_instalment_eur): each quotient is worked out at scale 18 and then cut off toward zero at the T-SQL scale of 13 using floor(x, s) or ceil(x, s), with the target scale passed in. This needs PySpark 3.5 or later, so it's fine on 4.2. After that comes ROUND half-up, or a cut-off at 4 places for daily_rate_eur.

3) earned_pct and the instalment divisor both use the Spark expression 'div', which cuts the result off toward zero the way T-SQL integer division does. A term_days of 0 raises a division error, as the legacy job does.

4) The latest-FX-rate lookup is grouped per source row (premium_transactions._row_seq), not per txn_id, because txn_ids are never deduplicated. Duplicate txn_ids, or a policy with more than one current dim_policy row, would give duplicate keys. The legacy job would fail on its primary key in that case.

5) Currency and is_current comparisons ignore case and trailing spaces. The output currency is padded to 3 characters. Reading with NOLOCK can change results from run to run, which the migration can't reproduce.
